title: Seiko: Why did a ¥450,000 watch still need factory adjustment?｜Brand Story
description:
Why could a new quartz watch keep accurate time yet still need to go back to the factory for adjustment? We follow hand-soldered boards under microscopes in the late 1960s, smaller resonators and motors, the 1969 shipment and price change, aging and furnace checks, then later divider chips and repairable connections described in a 1977 technical paper.

Launch and manufacturing events follow Seiko/Epson retrospectives, excerpts from the 2004 company history, Shigeru Aoki's 2017 technical history and Hideaki Yasukawa's 1977 paper, preserving each period and attribution. Multiple returned watches are not combined into one traceable serial-number case. The 20% figure is early resonator production yield; 10% is the usable IC selection proportion at a particular stage, not a return rate. Accuracy retains its normal-temperature conditions; the car-price comparison uses only the 1966 Tokyo Corolla Standard. The initial hybrid circuit, the purchased Intersil divider chip for the 35SQ, the in-house Type A and December 1971 38 series, and the assembly described in 1977 remain distinct in model and period. We do not adopt the old single-cause account of Swiss industry or the claim of free patents worldwide. Images are anonymous conceptual illustrations.

chapters.skr1e01: Fitting a resonator, circuits and a motor into 3 cm
chapters.skr1p01: Delivered to Tokyo, but the price tag changes again

chapters.skr1c01: From hand-soldered circuits to the next generation of chips
chapters.skr1d01: Smaller circuits still need room for repair

skr1h01.text: In 1969, even if you spent ¥450,000 on a watch, you might still have to send it back for adjustment.

skr1h02.text: Seiko's company history records this early problem; in the late 1960s, skilled workers were still hand-soldering circuits under microscopes.

skr1h03.text: The circuit on a ceramic board had to fit into a tiny movement alongside the battery and gears.

skr1h04.text: I focus first on that soldering iron: after making one watch, could they make the next one the same way?

skr1h05.text: Why would a price tag suddenly change the preparations for launch?

skr1h06.text: And what unrecorded detail lay hidden in a vacuum furnace at the factory?

skr1h07.text: Follow Seiko's Astron from a hand-soldered board to see how a new watch moved toward sustained production.

skr1h08.text: Once accuracy fits on a wrist, what else must be done before handing it to the next person?

skr1e01.text: What you hand over is a wristwatch that moves as you walk and raise your arm, and whose battery you will replace.

skr1e02.text: Start with the resonator deep inside; here, it gives the circuit a steady beat.

skr1e03.text: A 2017 technical history records that the team chose tuning-fork-shaped quartz.

skr1e03a.text: No ready-made resonator suitable for a wristwatch was available on the market then, so the team had to try machining one themselves.

skr1e03b.text: The technical history says they tried abrasives and vibration, and finally made the tuning-fork shape using a grinding stone.

skr1e04.text: But if you shrink a piece of quartz, will other parts have to change too?

skr1e05.text: The retrospective says size and vibration frequency are linked: smaller means a higher frequency.

skr1e06.text: Faster vibration calls for more frequency-divider stages, making power consumption a problem too.

skr1e07.text: This model at the time used 8,192 vibrations per second.

skr1e08.text: The watch on your wrist moves around, so the little resonator cannot be allowed to knock about inside.

skr1e09.text: In the technical history's diagram, thin springs suspend it inside a small vacuum-sealed capsule.

skr1e10.text: Looking at those fine wires, I want to ask: once the beat is steady, can the hands move on their own?

skr1e11.text: That fast beat still has to be divided down to deliver a drive signal once per second.

skr1e12.text: This design uses 13 divider stages, each halving the frequency from the previous stage.

skr1e13.text: But how did they fit those circuits inside at the time?

skr1e14.text: Seiko's product history records a circuit with 76 transistors, 29 capacitors and other components.

skr1e15.text: The oscillator, divider and drive circuits formed a hybrid circuit.

skr1e16.text: Imagine soldering that tiny contact in your hand, then moving on to the next one.

skr1e17.text: But between the circuit sending a signal and the hands actually moving, there is still a motor.

skr1e18.text: If the motor draws power continuously, how can the little battery on your wrist last?

skr1e19.text: The technical history recounts how the team arranged three two-pole magnets at 60-degree intervals.

skr1e20.text: They applied drive pulses and saw the magnets turn, then tried shortening the time the power was on.

skr1e20a.text: The coil had to shrink too: about 20,000 turns of fine wire just 0.02 millimeters in diameter.

skr1e20b.text: When you put that wound wire back in the movement, you still need space for the other components.

skr1e21.text: The later six-pole motor received just one brief pulse per second, and its rotor moved 60 degrees per step.

skr1e21a.text: Power makes it turn, but when the power is off, could the rotor slip out of position?

skr1e22.text: When the current stops, attraction between the rotor and stator also helps hold it in place.

skr1e23.text: What interests me here is the cost in power of each step, rather than how fast it turns.

skr1e24.text: But with the motor ready, is there room to fit the whole thing inside a small watch?

skr1e25.text: The engineers separated the functional parts they could, distributing the coil, stator and rotor through gaps in the movement.

skr1e26.text: If you only look at the dial, you see the second hand advance step by step; the components inside are spread out.

skr1e27.text: With space saved, the movement could fit within a round frame; Seiko's data lists an outside diameter of 30 millimeters.

skr1e28.text: But that is the movement's size, and the section containing the battery is thicker than the rest.

skr1e28a.text: When it is time to change the battery, where do you open it?

skr1e28b.text: Seiko's product history specifically mentions a battery-hatch design that made replacement easier.

skr1e29.text: So when could this assembly on the workbench actually be sent out?

skr1p01.text: Before shipping, each watch still had to be ready for its final adjustment.

skr1p02.text: The company history dates the next scene to December 24, 1969.

skr1p03.text: As technical manager Hideaki Yasukawa hurried to Tokyo, ten quartz wristwatches had already been sent out.

skr1p04.text: Another ten were scheduled to arrive by the next morning; work at the factory was still unfinished.

skr1p05.text: I had thought this was a Christmas launch planned well in advance, but the retrospective says it was not.

skr1p06.text: Only at this point did there finally seem to be a chance of assembling enough watches.

skr1p07.text: If you were preparing tomorrow's presentation and the watches had arrived, could you simply put out the printed price tags?

skr1p08.text: The retrospective says the sales manager briefly changed the price to ¥380,000.

skr1p09.text: He felt that a price high enough to buy a mass-market car was simply too much.

skr1p10.text: How much money was that? First, you need to check the car's year and trim level.

skr1p11.text: In 1966, Toyota announced a Tokyo price of ¥432,000 for the Corolla Standard.

skr1p12.text: The Deluxe on the same price list was ¥495,000.

skr1p13.text: For the same watch, sales had changed the price, but who would make the final decision?

skr1p14.text: Back at the price tags being prepared, the company history says Shoji Hattori arrived that evening, looked at them and ordered the price restored to ¥450,000.

skr1p15.text: What I wonder is who would have to deal with that change next.

skr1p16.text: Staff had to replace the tags and redo printed materials; even working late into the night, they could not finish in time.

skr1p17.text: The press conference, originally set for 10 a.m. the following day, was therefore moved to 2 p.m.

skr1p19.text: The next day, the Astron officially went on sale; high accuracy was what it promised its buyers.

skr1p20.text: Seiko lists a monthly accuracy of plus or minus five seconds, under normal-temperature conditions from 4 to 36 degrees Celsius.

skr1p21.text: After you took the watch away from the counter, would that accuracy stay on your wrist?

skr1r01.text: The product left the counter, but it did not disappear from the factory's work list.

skr1r02.text: That company history records that aging of the early quartz resonators caused unstable accuracy.

skr1r03.text: As for the returns for adjustment you worried about at the start, the company history says many watches already sold did indeed come back for adjustment.

skr1r04.text: If it were yours, you would probably want to know: why could it change after being adjusted before it left?

skr1r05.text: I want to look back at the bench where the resonators were made; the issue went beyond that final adjustment.

skr1r06.text: The retrospective says cutting and grinding the quartz pieces left tiny cracks on the surface.

skr1r07.text: They had to deal with those cracks to have a chance of raising the usable proportion.

skr1r08.text: But is a surface that looks smooth enough to put your mind at ease?

skr1r09.text: Even after etching away a surface layer, you cannot tell by eye how many cracks remain.

skr1r10.text: Imagine adjusting the resonator's tips to the required frequency; the work cannot stop there.

skr1r11.text: Once power is actually applied and it keeps vibrating, the cracks change, and the frequency may shift too.

skr1r12.text: Some stabilized quickly, while others never settled down.

skr1r13.text: Only when I read this did I understand: being accurate at the moment of adjustment cannot stand in for the time that follows.

skr1r14.text: So how could the factory bring out that variation before shipping?

skr1r15.text: The company history records continuous power for several days, letting the resonators undergo aging and stabilization first.

skr1r16.text: Experience had to build up little by little on how much each one changed, and for how long.

skr1r17.text: In this early period, the retrospective says resonator production yield was only 20%.

skr1r18.text: Do not read that as 80% of watches being returned; this number is the usable proportion of resonators produced.

skr1r19.text: If the completed resonators were still unstable, what more could you learn just waiting beside the finished pieces?

skr1r20.text: This time, we need to follow the managers to where the processing actually happened.

skr1f01.text: One processing step was baking: quartz pieces went into a vacuum furnace, where heat removed gases contained inside.

skr1f02.text: If those gases were not properly removed, the vibration frequency could change, causing timekeeping errors too.

skr1f03.text: Watching the furnace run, would you assume it was heating as specified, or check the settings again?

skr1f04.text: As for the vacuum furnace at the start, the company history says managers found the problem only by checking operations on site.

skr1f05.text: The heating temperature had actually been set 50 degrees lower than it should have been.

skr1f07.text: Hearing this, I want to find the data kept at the time: did anyone record each setting?

skr1f08.text: The retrospective considers the bigger issue to be that the temperature settings had not been recorded as data.

skr1f10.text: If you took over the next shift without that record, where would you check what the previous shift had done?

skr1f11.text: This incident made on-site checks, records and clearly written work procedures lessons for the factory to remember.

skr1f12.text: But a steadier supply of resonators still did not make hand-soldered circuits easy to build.

skr1f13.text: If you wanted the next batch made faster, could you keep relying on the same number of tiny contacts?

skr1c01.text: Seiko commissioned the American company Intersil to develop low-power chips to replace hand-soldered circuitry.

skr1c02.text: The company history says hybrid circuits had very low productivity, and both cost and power consumption still needed to come down.

skr1c03.text: What I wonder is: if they could draw a circuit, why not simply replace it with a chip?

skr1c04.text: They needed both the design and the ability to manufacture it; at the time, the two were not ready together.

skr1c05.text: Meanwhile, Seiko also began building its own semiconductor manufacturing capability.

skr1c07.text: And when Intersil's chips later arrived, could every one be used to specification?

skr1c08.text: Quality and performance varied; the retrospective says only about 10% could be selected for use at that stage.

skr1c09.text: You need usable components before you can fit them into watches batch after batch; receiving a box does not solve everything.

skr1c22.text: Look at the original Astron model: when a purchased Intersil chip was later fitted, was the entire circuit replaced?

skr1c23.text: No; the company history says that CMOS chip handled only frequency division, while the other circuits retained a hybrid construction.

skr1c24.text: After the most complex divider section was changed, this watch needed fewer assembly operations and consumed less power.

skr1c10.text: I want to follow the in-house path: how did people who made precision machinery begin making semiconductors?

skr1c11.text: The company history records a group of young engineers starting with the basics of electronics and semiconductors.

skr1c11a.text: They invited electronics scholars to give intensive lectures and sent people to research institutions for training.

skr1c11b.text: They built their understanding step by step, starting with properties of insulating films.

skr1c11c.text: Hearing the principles was not enough; what could they show researchers to explain the problems they were facing?

skr1c12.text: In the retrospective, Yamamura also took a prototype to Tarui, a semiconductor researcher.

skr1c13.text: He described it as a soldered monster that could not yet fit into a wristwatch.

skr1c14.text: But what he wanted to convey was that the team hoped to move from that state to the next level.

skr1c15.text: Imagine the little watch beside that large circuit; the gap would take more than a different case to close.

skr1c16.text: There was also the manufacturing environment: they converted a laboratory into a cleanroom, then brought in semiconductor manufacturing equipment.

skr1c17.text: But when equipment arrives, does manufacturing know-how come with it?

skr1c18.text: The retrospective says their lack of manufacturing experience meant repeated experiments, and progress was difficult.

skr1c19.text: It was not until April 1971, the company history records, that the in-house Type A chip finally worked as intended.

skr1c20.text: An area smaller than five square millimeters contained frequency division and motor-drive signal output functions.

skr1c26.text: The company history says the in-house Type A chip went into the 38 series, launched in December 1971.

skr1c26a.text: Would you use the power saved for longer running time, or for a smaller battery?

skr1c26b.text: The company history presents both routes: keep the same battery and gain more running time.

skr1c26c.text: Or keep the original battery-life requirement and use a smaller battery to make the watch thinner.

skr1c27.text: But if you bought the next generation, who could take care of it when it failed?

skr1d01.text: In a 1977 technical paper, Hideaki Yasukawa extended the requirements to the retail side.

skr1d02.text: Even in the event of a failure, retailers should be able to make necessary repairs using simple jigs.

skr1d03.text: I want to look first at the connections he documented: as things get smaller, are there fewer places to work on?

skr1d04.text: The paper cites a later high-end quartz watch whose circuit assembly was designed with after-sales maintenance in mind.

skr1d05.text: That circuit used techniques such as precision stamping, bending and microwelding instead of soldered joints.

skr1d06.text: He specifically wrote that components such as capacitors and resistors could be replaced individually.

skr1d07.text: If a small component failed in this design, you would have a chance to deal with just that component.

skr1d08.text: Next, I want to know how those connections were assembled in batches at the factory.

skr1d09.text: The same paper includes a photograph: circuit assemblies were handled by a rotary, fully automatic assembly machine.

skr1d10.text: The machine capacity given in the paper was about 100,000 circuit units per month.

skr1d11.text: Remember the soldering iron at the beginning? In just a few years, both manufacturing tools and connection methods had changed.

skr1d12.text: But between assembling a circuit and shipping a complete watch, what else needed checking?

skr1d13.text: Yasukawa's account of quality assurance starts with the reliability of every electronic component.

skr1d14.text: Once assembled into a product, timekeeping accuracy, operation and display performance also needed examination.

skr1d15.text: Temperature characteristics were part of this too; when you use your watch in a different environment, its electronic mechanism still faces changes.

skr1d16.text: Reading this page takes my question beyond accuracy to whether it can be made consistently and repaired easily.

skr1d17.text: These later circuits and methods each belonged to their own models; they did not all appear in the first batch of watches.

skr1d18.text: My answer is: to put accuracy into the next person's hands, stability, manufacturing and repair all have to be addressed too.

skr1d19.text: Tell me in the comments: when you choose a new tool, what would you most like to worry less about—accuracy, repair or price?

skr1d20.text: To keep seeing how everyday objects go from something we can make to something people can use, subscribe to Brand Stories.
